summary: Explains why an OSPF Area Border Router needs a working connection to the backbone area if it is to route traffic to other areas and to outside destinations. Traffic for other areas is dropped otherwise. It then describes alternative ABR behaviors implemented in Cisco and IBM routers. It is informational and documents implementation practice.

eli5.summary: A big city is split into neighborhoods, and a few roads connect them to the main highway. This memo explains that a connecting road must really reach the highway, or cars cannot get anywhere else, and it lists other ways to build one.

questions: ospf area border router without backbone connection
what is an ospf abr without backbone connection
why does an abr drop traffic in ospf
do ospf virtual links need a backbone
subtitle: Two vendor behaviors that keep an OSPF router with no backbone link from dropping transit traffic.

tldr.problem: Under the base OSPF rules, a router attached to several areas but not to the backbone calls itself an Area Border Router (ABR) yet cannot learn inter-area routes, so it drops traffic bound for the backbone and other areas.
tldr.mechanism: The alternative behaviors let a router claim to be an ABR only with an active backbone connection, and let it consider summary-LSAs from all attached areas when it lacks one.
tldr.outcome: These behaviors, implemented in Cisco and IBM routers, are compatible with standard OSPF, but can cause asymmetric routing.

today: RFC 3509 is an Informational RFC and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents vendor behavior and notes that those implementations are subject to future change.

sections.title: The Problem With a Backbone-less ABR
sections.content:
An OSPF domain is split into areas, which limit the scope of LSA flooding. A router attached to several areas is an area border router (ABR). Its main job is to give its areas Type-3 and Type-4 LSAs, which describe routes and AS boundary routers in other areas, and to do the actual inter-area routing. Standard OSPF (RFC 2328) does not require an ABR to be attached to the backbone (area 0).

The memo explains why that is a trap. An ABR only examines summary-LSAs from the backbone when building its routing table. With no backbone connection it has only intra-area routes. Yet it still sets the B bit in its router-LSA and so attracts traffic. An internal router in a neighboring area may find its best path to the backbone runs through this ABR, which then drops everything not destined for its directly attached areas. The same happens when a backbone-connected ABR loses all its backbone adjacencies.

Virtual links can repair this, but add configuration work and system traffic overhead. A second case is a dual-homed customer router reached through several areas, which standard ABR behavior also handles poorly.
sections.eli5: A junction that says it joins the highway but does not really do so will swallow any car that tries to use it as a shortcut.

sections.title: The Alternative ABR Behaviors
sections.content:
The idea is that a router connected to multiple areas without a backbone connection is not an ABR and should act as an internal router in every attached area, as if separate OSPF processes ran for each area. The memo defines terms first: a configured area has at least one interface assigned to it, an actively attached area has an interface not in the Down state, and an active backbone connection means the backbone is actively attached and has at least one fully adjacent neighbor.

The two vendor interpretations differ in when a router is an ABR:

  • Cisco: more than one area actively attached, and one of them is the backbone.
  • IBM: more than one area actively attached, and the backbone area configured.

Three changes are made to base OSPF. The B bit in the router-LSA is set only once the router is an ABR under these definitions. The routing table calculation considers summary-LSAs from all actively attached areas if the router is not an ABR or has no active backbone connection. For the Cisco approach, summary-LSA origination changes so a router without an active backbone connection announces only intra-area routes, which prevents loops of summary-LSAs.
sections.eli5: The rule is simple: only call yourself a junction if you really touch the highway. Otherwise, listen to every neighborhood's directions so you can pass cars along.

sections.title: Virtual Links
sections.content:
The Cisco approach requires an ABR to have at least one active interface in the backbone area. That is a problem when the backbone is purely virtual, as in the memo's example of two routers joined only by a virtual link. Under the base rules, the virtual link never comes up, because neither router-LSA carries the B bit and neither router has an active backbone interface.

The memo calls this situation rare and suggests that implementations supporting the Cisco behavior may report a virtual link up when the router with the matching router ID is seen in the Dijkstra calculation, whether or not its router-LSA says it is an ABR. The problem does not appear if one of the routers has a real backbone interface.

The memo also states that these methods do not remove the need for virtual links when an area has no physical backbone connection at all.
sections.eli5: If the only link to the highway is an imaginary one, both junctions wait for the other to go first. The fix is to believe the link is up once you can see the other end.

sections.title: Compatibility and Deployment
sections.content:
The changes do not affect router-to-router cooperation and do not create routing loops, so the memo calls them fully compatible with standard OSPF. It says a proof of compatibility is outside its scope. Standard and alternative ABRs can coexist in one domain.

The memo warns about routing asymmetry. In its example, a router R3 with the alternative behavior keeps an intra-area route toward network N, so traffic from network M to N crosses areas directly through R3, while traffic from N to M goes through the backbone. The memo adds that the problem is not caused by the alternative approach itself. R3 simply is not functioning as a real ABR, since it injects no summary-LSAs, yet inter-area traffic can still pass through it.
sections.eli5: The tweaks work fine with ordinary routers. One quirk: cars may go one way by a shortcut and come back by the highway.

sections.title: Disclaimer and Implementations
sections.content:
The memo says it describes the vendors' implementations as is, for information only, and that the authors do not intend to keep it in sync with the implementations. It records versions: an initial Cisco implementation, slightly different from the one described, was introduced in Cisco IOS 11.1(6), and the behavior described in the memo was integrated in version 12.1(3)T. The IBM approach was implemented in IBM Nways Multiprotocol Routing Services (MRS) 3.3.

For security, the memo says the alternative behaviors raise no issues beyond those already covered in RFC 2328.
sections.eli5: The authors are just reporting what two companies already do. They are not promising it will stay the same.
